text_fidelity_a:
idea display Q32P 32" IPS 4K UHD Gaming Monitor, 3840x2160, 60Hz OD4ms, 100% sRGB, 1xHDMI,1xDisplayport, 2xUSB,Type-C, USB-B, Remote Control, Frameless FreeSync HDR, LED Backlight I selected this monitor to work on a beefy laptop I use for building Linux virtual machines and testing software, so my use case is a little different than the target audience. I have been needing a larger monitor to go with said laptop and this one seemed to be a good one. So far I am pleased with it, though I have not pushed it to its full potential.

This is a 27" display capable of 2560x1440 resolution, fast refresh rates and bright colors. In the box comes the panel itself, a stand, and a DisplayPort cable. I was a little surprised that there was no HDMI cable in the box but this is all right, I have a couple of them so I was not left wanting.

My initial testing was disastrous, though the issue proved to be a fault with the laptop, not the monitor. My laptop has an HDMI output, and it does provide enough power to let the monitor know that something is there, but it intermittently sends a signal so I was not getting a consistent display. After a couple of hours, the monitor would display nothing at all. Thinking I had a dud, I connected a different system to verify and the monitor came right up. It did the same with a second system as well. After some research I determined that the issue was the graphics card in my main laptop which has known problems with HDMI. I bought an adapter to connect to the Thunderbolt port on the laptop and everything works fine now.

The system connected to this monitor is a gaming laptop that is running Linux with VMs installed. The system properly reports the model number of the display which is a very good sign. The OS does not push the monitor like a Windows gaming system might when used for actual gaming. For me, the screen real estate is what I needed. The adapter I bought caps the resolution at 1920x1200, so I am not getting the full resolution from this monitor but it is more than enough for my purposes.

The monitor responds to signal on both HDMI ports. So far I have not had occasion to try using the DisplayPorts on the back.

The display is very bright and clear, with no dead pixels. It seems to keep up very well with the system with no apparent lag, though again I am not pushing it as hard as I could. Because of the way I have it connected I can't bump up the refresh rate though it is happy at 60Hz. It doesn't appear to flicker to my eyes (though my camera disagrees), and it does not induce headaches.

If I could make any changes at all, I would change the design of the stand/base. The base is not height-adjustible so I cannot raise or lower the monitor without getting an arm harness. That's a minor complaint and is not enough to get myself upset about but it is worth mentioning.

Admittedly I am not the typical use case for a monitor like this, but I am happy with it nonetheless and it works well for me. The issues I have had with this monitor were related to other hardware, not the monitor itself. It seems to work very well, it is bright and clear and it gives me the screen real estate that I need. The fact that the Linux system recognizes its model number is a plus - it's supported.
text_fidelity_b: idea display Q32P 32" IPS 4K UHD Gaming Monitor, 3840x2160, 60Hz OD4ms, 100% sRGB, 1xHDMI,1xDisplayport, 2xUSB,Type-C, USB-B, Remote Control, Frameless FreeSync HDR, LED Backlight

text_fidelity_a:
Ring Video Doorbell 2 with HD Video, Motion Activated Alerts, Easy Installation Back in 2016, I was getting into the Video Doorbells for extra security for packages. After much review of Ring, Skybell, Nest, and August doorbells, I decided to purchase the Skybell. I instantly enjoyed being able to get notifications when there was motion and when the button would be pressed. The advantage with Skybell was that it came with free subscription. Well... after 2 years of using the Skybell, i ran into many issues where the motion would not notify me or even pickup, wireless trying to connect to my network at home, and many other headaches which you would think be fixed after many patches. I have my own server room and network system which I ran network throughout my house and even have a business hotspot near the Skybell, still had many issues with the Skybell doorbell.

Moving forward......

I reviewed my options again as I was fed up with Skybell and still only had the same options today as they were 2 years ago. After much consideration i decided to choose the Ring Doorbell 2. They do offer a free subscription now, which is great, but you cannot review any motion or button press history events. Of course this is just due to needing to purchase the basic plan for the cloud storage. Even for $30 annually, the basic plan is still cost effective. After using the doorbell in the trial version of the plus plan, I am planning on paying the $30 just because its cheap cost and I would rather have the events to review rather than just seeing the live view.

Setup was easy (easier than Skybell). The app loads quick and can edit motion detection's, alerts, and much more. I connected the doorbell via hardwired to an analog doorbell. The box comes with many customization options, tools, and took only 10 minutes to install.

Testing the Ring doorbell worked perfectly and better than Skybell. I installed my Ring doorbell with the provided wedges that came in the box. I have a 20 foot driveway and the detection works so great that cars driving by alert me. You can decrease the range of the motion in the app. When there is motion, I can open the app from my lock-screen and only takes about 2 to 3 seconds before i can see the event. The load times are very quick and faster than Skybell.

Overall, I am day 15 in my trial and I am glad I decided on Ring. The product is great, and far better than competitors. Cost is ideal for those that do not want to pay hundreds each year on cloud storage like nest. I would highly recommend Ring to others.
text_fidelity_b: Ring Video Doorbell 2 with HD Video, Motion Activated Alerts, Easy Installation

Samsung 128GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive Fit (MUF-128BB/AM) I bought 2 of these, they came today, and I and am returning them both tomorrow.

Chief reason: the drive is so small, that it is hard to plug into either USB port in the back of my new TV, a Sony XBR 850C. That TV has a somewhat constricted space where all of its ports are (USB, HDMI, etc). I just learned the hard way that I really need a longer drive to easily insert/remove it with this TV. Anyone else in a similar situation should likewise give this drive a serious rethink. I note that I had little problem with inserting/removing this drive from the front of my workstation, where I have unrestricted space.

Secondary reason: this drive has poor write speeds. My first transfer was of a single 2 GB movie file--a pure sequential write, which should be optimal--and yet I got an initial speed that started at ~50 MB/s and then it decay to maybe 40 MB/s. I should have paid more careful attention to the write benchmarks of this drive. I really want >= 100 MB/s write speeds.

It looks like my best bet is this drive's bigger brother, the Samsung 32GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive MUF-32BA/AM. Ordering 2 right now, stay tuned...

text_fidelity_a:
Jabra EASYGO Bluetooth Headset [Retail Packaging] As a general rule, I hate hands-free handsets.

I hate it when I begin speaking with someone, and I think they're agreeing with everything I say, and then it turns out they're actually talking to someone else using their dratted ear extension with the flashing blue light.

I hate the fact that my ears are the wrong size and shape for the majority of headsets.

I hate it when my untrained (clumsy) fingers hit the wrong part of the headset when I'm simply trying to stop it from falling to its death from a height of just over 5 feet, and I either redial the last number or hang up on the one person who hates being hung up on.

Plus, they're UGLY, and don't accessorise well with any wardrobe!!

HOWEVER,

I hate it even more when I have to pull over and park to take or make a call.

And I especially hate it if I DON'T pull over, and then get busted by the only policeman on the entire empty highway who has insomnia and a full book of blank tickets waiting to be filled in.

SO,

Hands free it shall be -
But ONLY when I'm driving.

That said, this device fits most of my basic needs, and throws in some convenient extras. The EASYGO Headset was indeed very easy to set up and even easier to use. Sound quality was good and the spoken connection status and audio volume adjuster are useful features.

The headset is also relatively small and stylish (as hands-free headsets go) without any flashing lights or buttons that attract unwanted attention (or cause an attack of photosensitive epilepsy, or signal the letters N-E-R-D in morse code.)

The most impressive feature of this headset has to be the long battery life, which is great because the miserly charger cord is so awkward to use that you don't want to have to use it more often than necessary. Besides, as I only use it in the car, it lasts me several trips, depending on how often and how long I prattle.

Admittedly it is more comfortable to use than I expected. The extra ear hook prevents suicidal leaps from ear to earth, and it doesn't weigh my head down on one side.

In summary, for a simple headset, it delivers.

Rated: 4.5 stars

Amanda Richards
January 19, 2011

text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Basics On-Ear Headphones I use headphones very frequently under a number of different environments including noisy computer labs, airplanes, quiet rooms and more. I am particularly familiar with noise canceling phones but I do have a some non-ANC phones that I use for listening to music in quiet environments. This pair of Amazon Basics headphones is my least expensive pair but it actually compares reasonably well against some more expensive phones.

First, the Basics headphones are very lightweight on-ear phones. They are slightly tight though not so tight to cause discomfort. What they do cause for me is a bit of warmth on the ears, something that I have not experienced very often when using headphones. It’s a minor aggravation, not a show-stopper by any means.

The most important feature of any headphones is the sound profile. I like electronic music which has a wide range of sound frequency - abundant highs, full midrange and quite a bit of bass. When listening to tracks with these phones, the first thing that I could not help but notice is that they overdrive the bass a little much, but this seems to be more the norm with headphones anymore. The highs sound just about right - not exceptionally sharp but not muted either. The midrange, though, is off and reminds me of listening to music in a tunnel. It isn’t terrible, but it’s noticeable. From what I can tell, the bass is so overdriven that it partially flattens the midrange.

I compared these headphones to a pair of Munitio PRO40 phones, a much more expensive set ($350 full retail) of phones that I use for studio work. Yes, the Munitio phones outperformed the Basics phones, but the difference did not match the $300 price difference. Other than the midrange, the Basics phones compared very well on the sound spectrum. That’s more than I could have asked for at $15.

If this was an expensive set of phones I would be very upset. However, this is a VERY inexpensive set and for the price range sounds much better than average.

Construction-wise this set of phones feels well-made. They won’t hold up to abuse, but with proper care they should last a long time. They even come with a cloth carry bag with offers little more than scratch protection but it’s a nice touch.

Considering how inexpensive these headphones are, I am hard-pressed to criticize. In their price range they are well above average in terms of sound and construction. If you are looking for a lightweight and inexpensive set of headphones and you do not need the very best in sound this is an outstanding value.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Basics On-Ear Headphones

text_fidelity_a:
Acer Chromebook 15, Intel Celeron N3350, 15.6" Full HD Touch, 4GB LPDDR4, 32GB Storage, Google Chrome, Pure Silver, CB515-1HT-C2AE, 15-15.99 Inches I ordered the Acer Chromebook 15, Intel Celeron N3350, 15.6" Full HD Touch, 4GB LPDDR4, 32GB Storage, Google Chrome, Pure Silver, CB515-1HT-C2AE, 15-15.99 inches so that I might have a lightweight portable travel laptop to enjoy and use for travel and at home. I have had some time with the new Chromebook and I would like to share a few thoughts and experiences with this particular model.

The first thing that I noticed with this Acer Chromebook was how thin and lightweight it was. It reminded me of a Macbook, though I have never owned one. I love the silver metal look and the keyboard is very enjoyable and comfortable to use. The speakers on either side of the keyboard are nice and sound amazing considering the size and the fact that they are housed in a very thin and compact space.

Initially I did experience some issues with the screen where it would not turn on despite the fact that there was power. It was very random but about 80% of the time the display would not turn on. I was able to contact Acer and they did resolve the issue within a reasonable amount of time. I had to send it back to Acer and they replaced the mainboard which I assume was the culprit. As I type up this review I am doing so on the repaired Chromebook and I have to say that though I had that initial experience, Acer made it right and I absolutely love this product! I’m not real savvy with the Chromebook OS but it really is simple and I appreciate the fact that this model comes with a Micro SD slot for my 128gb card which will come in handy to use for loading some movies and or music for on-the-go. Also it will come in handy for loading a few photos to edit with my favorite mobile photo editing app using the excellent touch screen which I quite enjoy.

Speaking of movies I have played a bit with Netflix, Google Movies and Hulu and the video quality is quite amazing with the 1080p screen resolution and, as I mentioned earlier, the sound is surprisingly loud and clear.

Battery life has been pretty impressive and lasts much better than I expected. As I stated before, this has been my first Chromebook experience so the only thing I have to compare battery life with is my much larger gaming laptop which I can't even get a few hours of use before I need to plug in.

Overall this Acer Chromebook 15 has been quite enjoyable, and because of Acer’s great support, I would highly recommend this Chromebook if you are looking for an inexpensive well rounded mobile “Laptop” experience.
text_fidelity_b: Acer Chromebook 15, Intel Celeron N3350, 15.6" Full HD Touch, 4GB LPDDR4, 32GB Storage, Google Chrome, Pure Silver, CB515-1HT-C2AE, 15-15.99 Inches

text_fidelity_a: Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White We have all three of the Echo products: The Dot, The Tap, and the original Echo. The Dot works very similarly to the original Echo. You say the wake word, you give a command or question, it responds. It does have a speaker itself, but it doesn't get as loud as the original Echo or the Tap. All of the devices will sync together in one Amazon app, but they all still work independently. Meaning, if I set an alarm on the Dot, only the alarm on the Dot goes off. But with the app on my phone, I can access all the devices in the one place. The Original Echo is better for larger areas. the Dot is ideal if you already have a sound system you would like to connect the Dot to, or small spaces like bathrooms or bedrooms. The Dot is great for kids. My daughter has it in her room so she can ask it how to spell words and such. The Tap is an entirely different beast, in my opinion. No wake word. Touch and talk. But it works via Bluetooth and wifi for on the go use using your cellular device. The Echo Dot does not come with a remote. Like the Original Echo, it needs to be plugged into the wall and needs wifi. (The Tap has a chargeable battery.) They are all great devices, though Amazon still has some work to be done on them. Each has a different place where it is the ideal choice, so which you should choose really depends on your needs.

Conversely: 1 = much worse than expected. 2 = worse than expected. This New Stars Scale thus allows a negative rating as some have complained that they "Can't give negative 5 stars." Well now you can as 1 and 2 are in effect negative ratings, being lower than 3 which is essentially "OK. It works as expected, no better, no worse."

Well this mouse gets a New Stars Scale rating of only 2 because there is no way by glancing at it to tell if it is on or off. Rather one has to either 1) wiggle the mouse and see on the computer screen - if it is up and running - what the cursor does, or even if it is there or 2) pick up the mouse and look at the tiny black on/off switch on the bottom. Whether on or off, the tracking beam is invisible to the human eye.

Whereas my Amazon Basics mouse has a red jewel on top that lights up when it is on. Good idea! And it has a solid feel and better click. It is better then expected (or normal) so it gets a 4.

So I won't be buying the Logitech M170 mouse again.

Amazon Basics USB 3.1 Type-C to 4-Port Aluminum Hub Connector, Black One of the problems I have seen with the latest crop of notebooks and Ultrabooks that have come out is a lack of USB ports. There's usually a need for more ports than these systems have and it gets frustrating. A small USB hub like this is a good solution. That said, this particular hub does not have a separate power source so some consideration must be made when plugging in power-hungry devices.

From a design stantpoint this is a solid unit, shaped to be accessible without being huge. It has a little weight to it and this is helpful for keeping it stable. The addition of Velcro strips in the package to secure it in one place is a welcome inclusion and makes securing the hub very simple no matter what your configuration is.

The hub provides four USB 3.1 type A ports. Let me state what should be obvious - this will not convert a USB 1.1 or 2.0 port into a 3.1 port, so plug it into a 3.1 port if you want the speed across the hub. For my specific uses, it does not need to be a high-speed hub and I am find with using it as a 2.0 hub, but admittedly that's slightly wasteful.

There is no power port on this hub and there is no DC adapter in the box. So, any power that the hub needs comes through the onboard port into which it is plugged. That's fine for low-power devices like mice, keyboards, memory sticks and so on, but if the intent is to plug in such things as USB hard drives with no external power supply this can cause some headaches. No, one drive isn't going to overload the hub, but if you have multiple drives attached there may be reliability issues when they starve one another for power. When the device plugged in has its own power supply (like a big backup drive), this has little impact on the hub.

The point is, plan carefully how you intend to use the hub.

I like this hub and it does a good job for what it is. It has given me three extra ports on an Ultrabook I use which is all I could ask for. The ability to power this hub with it's own power supply would be the only area for improvement I could find.
